the car with time t for 6.0 s of its journey.

The brakes of the car are applied from t = 1.0 s to t = 4.0 s.
How far does the car travel while the brakes are applied?
A
21 m
B
45 m
C
67 m
D
83 m

hints: Notice the braking interval on the $t$-axis from $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ to $t = 4.0 \text{ s}$ and read the $v$-values at those two times, about $22 \text{m s}^{-1}$ falling to $8 \text{m s}^{-1}$.
Recall that on a velocity-time graph the displacement is the area under the graph, so the braking distance is the area of the trapezium between $1.0 \text{ s}$ and $4.0 \text{ s}$.
Find the average velocity during braking as $(22 + 8)/2$ and multiply by the $3.0 \text{ s}$ duration to get the distance in $\text{m}$.
walkthrough: Identify the braking section: the sloping straight line from $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ to $t = 4.0 \text{ s}$, so the time interval is $\Delta t = 4.0 - 1.0 = 3.0 \text{ s}$.
Read the velocities from the $v / \text{m s}^{-1}$ axis: initial velocity $u = 22 \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ and final velocity $v = 8 \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 4.0 \text{ s}$.
State the rule: displacement equals area under a velocity-time graph, and here the shape is a trapezium with parallel sides $u$ and $v$ and width $\Delta t$.
Calculate: average velocity $= 15 \text{m s}^{-1}$, so $s = 15 \times 3.0 = 45 \text{ m}$ with unit check $\text{m s}^{-1} \times \text{s} = \text{m}$.

A.explanation: Too small - about half the true area, possibly from using only the change in velocity $14 \text{m s}^{-1}$ instead of the actual velocities.

B.explanation: Area of the trapezium from $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ to $t = 4.0 \text{ s}$ with velocities $22 \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $8 \text{m s}^{-1}$ gives $45 \text{ m}$.

C.explanation: Too large - close to the distance for a longer time or a higher average velocity than the $15 \text{m s}^{-1}$ during braking.

D.explanation: Too large - similar to the total area from $t = 0$ to $t = 6.0 \text{ s}$, not just the braking interval $1.0 \text{ s}$ to $4.0 \text{ s}$.
